stage_name: Real hardware-in-the-loop: Development-mode Flash Encryption enabled for real on the connected ESP32-C6; found and fixed a second real stack-overflow bug (this time in this session's own S6 #7/#10/#11 work, start_production_https()); confirmed the production HTTPS listener's fail-closed certificate gate operates correctly end-to-end on real hardware for the first time
note_on_commits: No new commit created; commits are only made on explicit user request. Layered on top of all uncommitted S5/S6 work including HIL-persisted-state-stack-overflow-fix.json (the prior HIL finding in this same session).
sequencing_note: User asked 'де ж взяти TLS-сертифікат' (where to get a TLS certificate), which surfaced that the plan's own private-CA model requires loading real certificate material into S5's encrypted storage -- and that storage's write gate requires Flash Encryption to be genuinely verified active, which was off on this real chip. User was offered three options (test the validator in isolation with no hardware changes; enable Flash Encryption for real; stop); chose to enable it for real. Recon then found the project's OWN approved production profile (sdkconfig.production.esp32c6) bundles Release-mode Flash Encryption WITH Secure Boot V2 -- a materially higher, brick-capable risk not disclosed in the first framing. User was shown this new information explicitly and re-asked; chose the safer Development-mode-only path (no Secure Boot), explicitly rejecting both the full production bundle and stopping.
changed_files: components/web_ui/web_server.cpp (changed: start_production_https()'s three 4096-byte cert/key/CA buffers -- 12KB total -- converted from stack locals to `static`, fixing both a real stack overflow AND a latent dangling-pointer risk, see work_summary below)
frozen_decisions_applied: Flash Encryption enabled in DEVELOPMENT mode only (CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENC_ENABLED=y, CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENCRYPTION_MODE_DEVELOPMENT=y), explicitly NOT Release mode and explicitly NOT bundled with Secure Boot (CONFIG_SECURE_BOOT unset) -- a deliberate, informed deviation from this project's own approved sdkconfig.production.esp32c6 (which specifies Release mode + Secure Boot V2 together), chosen specifically to avoid the brick risk that combination carries, using a separate, temporary, session-scoped sdkconfig fragment (never committed, never touching the tracked sdkconfig.production.esp32c6).

CONFIG_ZGW_PRODUCTION_PROFILE=y was also set (this project's own app-level dev/prod switch, unrelated to ESP-IDF's security Kconfig) specifically so the HTTPS-listener/certificate-validation code path (Sections 2.7/2.10) would actually run on this real boot, without pulling in the rest of the production bundle.

CONFIG_PARTITION_TABLE_OFFSET=0x10000 and CONFIG_PARTITION_TABLE_CUSTOM_FILENAME="partitions.production.csv" were reused from the project's own already-verified production partition layout (the plain dev bootloader, once flash-encryption code is compiled in, no longer fits the default 0x8000 gap) -- reusing proven, already-correct data rather than improvising a new partition table.

The recovery from a mid-session operational mistake (see work_summary) used only ESP-IDF's own official `idf.py encrypted-flash` target, never a hand-rolled workaround, once the correct procedure was identified via real ESP-IDF `idf.py --help` output and the generated build-system args files -- not guessed.

flash_encryption_enabled_for_real.detail: First-ever real boot with CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENC_ENABLED=y: the bootloader's own automatic first-boot flash-encryption process ran successfully (real, observed log: 'Generating new flash encryption key...', 'bootloader encrypted successfully', 'partition table encrypted and loaded successfully', per-partition 'Encrypting partition N... Done encrypting', 'Flash encryption completed') and every subsequent boot confirms 'flash encryption is enabled (1 plaintext flashes left)'. esp_flash_encryption_enabled() -- and therefore this project's own hal_security_state_flash_encryption_enabled() -- now genuinely returns true on this real device for the first time.

second_real_stack_overflow_found_and_fix.status: COMPLETE -- found only because CONFIG_ZGW_PRODUCTION_PROFILE=y was exercised on real hardware for the first time ever
second_real_stack_overflow_found_and_fix.detail: With flash encryption active and CONFIG_ZGW_PRODUCTION_PROFILE=y set, the very next real boot crash-looped with the same 'Guru Meditation Error: Core 0 panic'ed (Stack protection fault)' signature as HIL-persisted-state-stack-overflow-fix.json's finding, but in a completely different, newer function: riscv32-esp-elf-addr2line pinpointed web_ui::(anonymous namespace)::start_production_https() at web_server.cpp:128, running on the 'main' task (app_main()'s own task, only ~4KB of stack) rather than 'service_runtime'. Root cause: three 4096-byte stack-local buffers (cert_bytes/key_bytes/ca_bytes, for the certificate/private-key/CA PEM data read from storage) -- 12KB total, three times the entire task's stack budget. This function had been written, reviewed, cppcheck'd, arch-invariant-checked and compile-and-link-verified via two separate real idf.py builds earlier in this same session (S6-tls-certificate-validation-completion.json) -- none of those checks exercise runtime stack usage, so this was invisible until the code actually ran, which had never happened before this exact moment (CONFIG_ZGW_PRODUCTION_PROFILE was compile-verified but never previously booted on real hardware). Fixed identically to the first HIL finding: the three buffers moved to `static` storage (verified safe: start_production_https() has exactly one call site, called exactly once from app_main() on the single 'main' task at boot). This fix is ALSO required for correctness independent of the stack-overflow risk: `config.servercert`/`config.prvtkey_pem` (assigned a few lines later) are raw pointers into these buffers, and it was not confirmed via recon whether esp_https_server's own internal handling makes a durable copy the way mbedtls_x509_crt_parse() does -- `static` guarantees the buffers outlive the function call regardless, which a stack-local never could even if it had fit within budget.

operational_recovery_from_a_real_mistake.status: COMPLETE -- real incident, real recovery, no data loss, documented for future sessions
operational_recovery_from_a_real_mistake.detail: After enabling flash encryption, a second firmware update was flashed using a hand-copied `esptool.py write_flash` command (the exact command idf.py's OWN build output had printed at the end of the FIRST build, before flash encryption was ever active) -- this command lacked the `--encrypt` flag. The device's ROM download-mode bootloader accepted the write and reported 'Hash of data verified', but because flash encryption was already active, the plaintext bytes were written into flash the chip's transparent read-side decryption hardware then tried to decrypt as if they were ciphertext, producing garbage ('invalid header: 0xd54f9e66', looping indefinitely at the ROM's first-stage bootloader validation, before any of this project's own code ever ran). The device remained fully responsive to esptool's ROM download-mode protocol throughout (confirmed via a plain, read-only `chip_id` query) -- never bricked, always recoverable. Root cause confirmed via `esptool write_flash --help` (`--encrypt`: 'Apply flash encryption when writing data') and `idf.py --help` (revealing the correct, official `encrypted-flash` action, 'Flash the encrypted project' -- not discovered by guessing, found by reading the real tool's own documentation). Recovery: `idf.py -B <dir> -p /dev/ttyACM0 encrypted-flash`, confirmed via its own printed esptool invocation to include `--encrypt` and to rewrite all four affected regions (bootloader, partition table, ota_data, app). The device booted cleanly afterward with zero further errors.

fail_closed_gate_verified_end_to_end.status: COMPLETE -- first real confirmation this gate works, not just compiles
fail_closed_gate_verified_end_to_end.detail: After both fixes, the device booted cleanly through Wi-Fi AP start, mDNS start (correctly logging 'https://zigbee-gateway-fffe9f.local', confirming the Section 2.8/2.9 CONFIG_ZGW_PRODUCTION_PROFILE branch is live), and service_runtime task start, then real log lines confirmed the exact intended fail-closed behavior: 'secure_storage: read key="tls_cert_cur" status=1' (SecureStorageStatus::kNotProvisioned) -> 'web_server: Production HTTPS listener: current certificate unavailable -- refusing to start (fail closed)' -> 'app_main: Web server start failed' (app_main.cpp's own existing halt-on-critical-failure logic, unchanged, taking over cleanly). Zero panics, zero reboots -- the device sits in a clean, deliberate halt state exactly as designed, for the first time ever demonstrating on real hardware that the whole chain built across S6-https-listener-completion.json/S6-tls-certificate-validation-completion.json (storage read -> presence check -> fail closed) works correctly, not just that it compiles.

hardware_in_the_loop.detail: This entire evidence file's finding is itself a real-hardware-only result: five full flash+boot+serial-capture round-trips against the actual connected ESP32-C6 across this HIL round (initial flash-encryption-enable boot -> crash discovered -> fix built -> incorrect manual reflash attempt -> corruption discovered -> bootloader-only reflash attempt (insufficient) -> correct `encrypted-flash` recovery -> clean boot confirmed with the fail-closed gate firing as designed).

environment_note: Continues directly from HIL-persisted-state-stack-overflow-fix.json's real-hardware environment (same device, same access mechanics -- see that file and the esp32c6-hardware-available memory note for the /dev/ttyACM0 Docker --device access pattern). New tooling used this round, all real and confirmed via the tools' own --help output or generated build-system files, never guessed: `esptool.py write_flash --encrypt`, `idf.py encrypted-flash`/`idf.py bootloader-flash`, and reading a build directory's own generated `*_flash_args` response files to see exactly which flags a given idf.py action actually passes to esptool (since the printed command line alone can omit flags folded into an `@args_file` reference).
unresolved_deviations: Real TLS certificate/private-key/CA material has still not been generated or loaded onto this device -- the fail-closed gate was confirmed correct precisely because nothing is loaded yet. Generating a real private CA + per-device leaf certificate (with the plan's own exact DNS/URI SAN requirements) and building a way to actually write it into the now-genuinely-encrypted NVS storage remains the next step toward observing the HTTPS listener's full positive path, not yet attempted.

This device now has Flash Encryption permanently, irreversibly active in Development mode. Any FUTURE reflash of this device (by this session or any future one) MUST use idf.py's encryption-aware actions (`encrypted-flash`, `encrypted-app-flash`, or plain `idf.py flash`/`idf.py app-flash` -- ordinary `idf.py flash` was NOT the cause of the corruption incident here, only the hand-copied raw esptool.py command was; idf.py's own actions correctly handle encryption when the current sdkconfig has it configured) -- never a hand-copied esptool.py command from before encryption was enabled. Recorded in the esp32c6-hardware-available memory file for future-session visibility.

The temporary HIL sdkconfig fragment used throughout this round (Flash Encryption Development mode + CONFIG_ZGW_PRODUCTION_PROFILE=y + production partition table) was never committed to the tracked repository and was not preserved as a file after this session's build directories were cleaned up -- if a future session needs to reproduce this exact HIL configuration, it will need to be reconstructed from this evidence file's frozen_decisions_applied section.
